clue.text: One dines badly in prison

parts.note: the Roman numeral for one is I

indicators.note: done badly, the letters of dines are jumbled into a new order

explanation.surface: A convict complains that one eats poorly behind bars.
explanation.walkthrough: 'badly' is the anagram signal for dines; 'in prison' reads as part of the story but is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone serving time is locked up, colloquially on the inside.

clue.text: Intrinsic in Tensing's first big climb

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: first picks the opening letter of Tensing's
in a down entry a word that climbs is read upwards, so backwards

parts.note: big means large

explanation.surface: Tenzing's first big ascent was central to his life.
explanation.walkthrough: 'climb' turns LARGE upwards to EGRAL in this down entry. Tensing (Tenzing Norgay) climbed Everest.
explanation.definitionFit: Integral and intrinsic both mean essential, built into the whole.

clue.text: Stung by clever journalist

parts.note: smart means clever
ED, short for editor, is the crossword journalist

explanation.surface: A reporter was hurt by a sharp-witted reporter's remark.
explanation.definitionFit: To smart is to feel a sharp sting, so smarted means hurt like a sting.

clue.text: That's Isolde adrift on the lake — a moving spirit

indicators.note: adrift means floating loose, so the letters wander into a new order

parts.note: ie, id est, means that is

explanation.surface: Wagner's heroine floats on a lake, a stirring soul.
explanation.walkthrough: 'adrift' rearranges IE plus ISOLDE into DIESELOI; L for lake goes on the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A fuel is a spirit in the sense of a volatile liquid, and this one powers moving engines.

clue.text: Substitute horse is odds-on as a jumper

indicators.note: one piece placed on, i.e. before, the other in the across entry

parts.note: SP, the starting price, is the betting odds on a horse
a ringer is a horse fraudulently swapped in for another in a race

explanation.surface: A racing tip about a swapped horse that bookmakers have made favourite in a steeplechase.
explanation.walkthrough: 'odds-on' looks like racing jargon for a favourite, but splits: the odds go on the substitute horse, a ringer.
explanation.definitionFit: Anything that springs or leaps is a springer; also a breed of spaniel bred to flush game.

clue.text: On the faculty for singing and dancing, say

definitions.text: On the faculty for singing and dancing, say

parts.words: On the faculty for singing and dancing, say
parts.note: a college department covering stage pursuits such as music, drama and dance; the phrase also suggests a stage act going on

explanation.surface: A college department teaching song and dance.
explanation.walkthrough: Singing and dancing are examples ('say') of the stage disciplines a faculty of this name teaches.
explanation.definitionFit: Music, dance and drama performed before an audience are grouped under this collective name.

clue.text: That is the date on the head of the tombstone

parts.note: the Ides is a date in the Roman calendar, as the Ides of March

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A gravestone's top carries a date.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' puts IDES above T in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin phrase abbreviated ie means precisely that is.

clue.text: It may spell danger to an oriental

definitions.text: It may spell danger to an oriental

indicators.note: letters that may spell something else can be rearranged into a new word

parts.note: E for East is oriental

explanation.surface: A bomb poses a threat to an Easterner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'may spell' rearranges DANGER into GRENAD; E for oriental goes on the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A bomb thrown by hand is a deadly threat to anyone, an Easterner included.

clue.text: Like some old boroughs, falling to pieces

explanation.surface: Historic towns crumble into ruin.
explanation.walkthrough: Before 1832 'rotten boroughs' were British constituencies with almost no voters still returning MPs.
explanation.definitionFit: The pre-1832 electoral districts were called this; and decayed, crumbling things are also described so.

clue.text: Plâtre

parts.note: the French word for gypsum plaster, the kind made from material quarried near the French capital

explanation.surface: A single French word.
explanation.walkthrough: Plâtre is French for plaster; the English name for the gypsum kind credits the French capital.
explanation.definitionFit: Plâtre is the French word, and the English name of fine gypsum plaster cites Paris as its source.

clue.text: "Farewell, Monsieur ___ : look you lisp" (A.Y.L.I.)

parts.note: a quotation from As You Like It, where Rosalind mocks the melancholy Jaques for his affected foreign airs after his journeys abroad

explanation.surface: A gap-fill quotation from Shakespeare's As You Like It.
explanation.walkthrough: Rosalind's line in Act 4 mocks Jaques as one who has journeyed abroad and come back lisping and wearing strange suits.
explanation.definitionFit: Jaques is addressed as a man who has journeyed widely, a voyager, which is the missing word.

clue.text: Lady not disheartened by this result

parts.note: Eve, the first woman, is a stock crossword lady

indicators.note: losing its heart, the word not drops its middle letter

explanation.surface: A woman is cheered rather than downcast by how things turned out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'disheartened' takes the middle letter out of not; 'by this' only links to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An outcome or happening, as in 'in the event', is a synonym of result.

clue.text: Chicken with giblets removed

explanation.surface: A cook prepares a bird by taking out its innards.
explanation.definitionFit: Chicken means cowardly, lacking guts; and a bird with its offal taken out has literally had its guts removed.

clue.text: Shock at being dismissed before the right time

parts.note: a batsman dismissed in cricket is out
an age is a long period of time

explanation.surface: A batsman is stunned at being given out before his proper turn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dismissed' is a cricket sense: the batsman is out.
explanation.definitionFit: Outrage is the shock and anger felt at an affront.

clue.text: The sound of a typist

parts.note: a kind of typist works from recorded speech heard through headphones, so sound defines her

explanation.surface: The clatter of an office keyboard.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests keyboard clatter; the cryptic reading is the typist who types from recordings.
explanation.definitionFit: Audio means sound, and an audio typist transcribes from recordings.

clue.text: Hostilities in the mine site possibly

indicators.note: possibly signals that the letters of mine site could be arranged differently

explanation.surface: Feuds break out at a colliery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'possibly' rearranges MINE SITE; 'in the' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: Enmities are hatreds or hostile feelings between parties, plural like the definition.

clue.text: Bird veers towards Tyneside

parts.note: to veer is to turn
to means towards
Tyneside is in the North East of England, NE

explanation.surface: A bird swerves off towards Newcastle.
explanation.walkthrough: Tyneside is the area round Newcastle, in north-east England, so NE.
explanation.definitionFit: A turnstone is a wading shorebird that flips pebbles to find food.

clue.text: Divers means of clearing drains

explanation.surface: Various ways of unblocking a sink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Divers' reads as 'various', but means people who dive.
explanation.definitionFit: People who dive headlong are those who plunge; and the rubber suction cups used to unblock sinks share the name.

clue.text: Were Elsie, Lacie and Tillie so U?

definitions.text: Were Elsie, Lacie and Tillie so U?

parts.words: Were Elsie, Lacie and Tillie so U?
parts.note: in Alice in Wonderland the Dormouse tells of three sisters by these names who lived at the bottom of a treacle well; U is upper class

explanation.surface: Were three Victorian girls posh?
explanation.walkthrough: U means upper-class in British usage. The three sisters lived in a well, so they would be born of it, a pun on aristocratic birth.
explanation.definitionFit: Of noble or aristocratic family, which is what upper-class U describes.

clue.text: Graceful unfinished lamentation on a hill-dweller

indicators.note: unfinished means the word loses its final letter

parts.note: an elegy is a lament
an ant lives in an anthill

explanation.surface: A lovely but incomplete lament about a mountain person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unfinished' drops the last letter of the lament; 'on a' links, the first piece sitting on top of the second in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Elegant means stylish and refined in movement or appearance.

clue.text: Sort of theatre the Spanish reject

parts.note: repertory theatre is shortened to rep
el is Spanish for the

explanation.surface: A Spanish company turns down a kind of drama.
explanation.walkthrough: REP (repertory) is a British theatre type with a resident company.
explanation.definitionFit: To repel is to drive back or fend off, synonym of reject as a verb.

clue.text: Lords say the lifts are quiet

parts.note: p, piano, is the musical mark for quiet
lifts, as a verb, means raises

explanation.surface: Peers remark that the elevators are silent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lords say' is the definition: said aloud, Lords sounds like lauds, which means praises.
explanation.definitionFit: To laud is to extol, so lauds is a synonym, signalled by the sound of Lords.

clue.text: Rising fish accounts for beetle

indicators.note: in a down entry rising means reading upwards, so the pieces are turned around

parts.note: the bar is a name for the maigre, a sea fish
ACS is short for accounts

explanation.surface: An ascending fish takes over a beetle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rising' turns BAR plus ACS upwards, so BARACS becomes SCARAB.
explanation.definitionFit: The scarab is a dung beetle, sacred in ancient Egypt.

clue.text: Writer when in drink may become brighter

indicators.note: one piece goes inside the other, as the writer in a drink

parts.note: a cup is a drink, as in a punch-style cup
Edward Lear, writer of nonsense verse

explanation.surface: An author grows more cheerful after a few drinks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' is the container signal; Edward Lear is the Victorian nonsense poet, and 'clear up' is said of weather.
explanation.definitionFit: The weather clears when it brightens, a phrasal-verb synonym.

clue.text: Material for the artist over there

parts.note: RA is a Royal Academician, an artist
yon means over there

explanation.surface: Supplies for a painter in the distance.
explanation.walkthrough: RA, a member of the Royal Academy, is the stock crossword artist.
explanation.definitionFit: Rayon is a synthetic fabric, a kind of cloth.

clue.text: Refrain from giving a second class mark

parts.note: B is the second grade or class
a stain is a mark

explanation.surface: A teacher holds back from awarding a B grade.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mark' looks like a school grade, but means STAIN; 'from giving' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: To abstain is to hold back or not take part, synonym of the verb refrain.

clue.text: Prepared to be like jolly tars always are

explanation.surface: Cheerful sailors are always on standby.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ready, aye, ready' is the Royal Navy's traditional motto, so tars (sailors) are always this.
explanation.definitionFit: Prepared is a plain synonym; and naval tradition has sailors always so, in their motto.

clue.text: Turned up in torn trousers with sweetheart

indicators.note: torn signals the letters of trousers being ripped apart and rearranged

parts.note: the heart of sweet is its middle letter E

explanation.surface: A lover in ripped trousers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'torn' rearranges TROUSERS into RETROUSS; 'sweetheart' gives E, the heart of SWEET.
explanation.definitionFit: Retroussé describes a nose tilted upward at the tip.

clue.text: Boat isn't ordered for Fuchs, say

indicators.note: ordered signals the letters of boat isn't being put into a new order

explanation.surface: A boat has not been commissioned for an explorer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fuchs' may suggest the Antarctic explorer Vivian Fuchs; it is Leonhart Fuchs, the plant scientist behind the fuchsia's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Leonhart Fuchs was a German scholar of plants, an example given by 'say'.

clue.text: Biblical divisions against Gaelic saint

parts.note: v, short for versus, means against
Erse is the Gaelic language

explanation.surface: Disputes over scripture set against an Irish saint.
explanation.walkthrough: V is versus, against; ERSE is a name for Gaelic.
explanation.definitionFit: The Bible is divided into chapters and numbered short sections, so each section is one of these.
